body:
Hi,

While the dialect will for sure need to be update to account for the change in aiosslite regarding the fact that the connection is no longer a thread, what you are seeing is kinda expected.

By default sqlalchemy uses connection pooling with aiosqlite so it does not close the connection when `async with engine.begin() as conn:` exits; the connection is instead returned to the pool.

So to fix this you can:
- disable connection pooling, using NullPool instead
- place a dispose call `await engine.dispose()` at the end of the `main` function so that all connections are correctly closed

Overall the main issue is that python gc destructor call has no way of doing async io, so you need to properly manage the connection yourself

I need to look at aiosqlite's new implementation (great news!) but we would also really benefit from having a non-async "terminate()" method of some kind so that when we detect that a connection has been thrown away (which we detect in a non-async weakref handler), we can ensure this connection is closed out without requiring the use of await.

FWIW, I was able to [fix the hang in my app](https://github.com/soliplex/soliplex/pull/319/files#diff-3dc849fde00b073f4118abfa2ae040fee37b288b848c4a1ff481bcd7c8e4feb9) by adding an `await engine.dispose()` at the end of my app's `lifetime` function. That change seems correct to me:  my code was previously skating with `aiosqlite < 0.22.0`.

by the time we get to where we are calling "terminate()", there should not be any event loop for us, which means if stop() does a hard stop without needing await in that case, that would be sufficient.  however it would be simpler if it did "stop without awaiting" in all cases becasue we wouldnt have to worry about a surprise awaitable there, but if that's not possible, not that big a deal.

the terminate case is when things have already gone wrong further up the chain so it's expected to be non-graceful.

so on the sqlalchemy side we could:
- check if the connection is a thread, and if not avoid `deamon=True`
- check if the connection has a `stop` method and use that for terminate if available 

alternatively we do these based on the driver version
@zzzeek do you prefer if the updated logic described here https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/13039#issuecomment-3668954805 is based on version number of on isinstance / hasattr?

aiosqlite v0.22.1 is released with the synchronous `stop()` function. It returns a future if the event loop is still open, but it is not necessary to await that future. Once `stop()` is called, the background thread will cleanup and terminate.

adding terminate does not really help. The only option to avoid leaving the thread open, thus making the close hanging is to set it as deamon.

Currently sqlalchemy does not do anything on engine/pool `__del__`. And even if it did in the example above the gc is not called before the runtime starts waiting for the threads.
If I add a `gc.collect()` after `asyncio.run(main())` then the pool and connections get gc-ed, without requiring any change in sqlalchemy part as of 0.22.1.
In 0.22.0 I get the same exception as the one reported, but I don't think it's fixable in sqlalchemy side even if it could call close on it, since there is no even loop in the gc thread.

Overall the best option is likely to just set the thread as deamon also in 0.22+. I'll also add terminate support since that was added.

The solution is that people need to call `await engine.dispose()` before terminating their programs, since io must be explicit with asyicion

**Federico Caselli** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **main** branch:

**Support aiosqlite 0.22.0+** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/6534

**Federico Caselli** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **rel_2_0** branch:

**Support aiosqlite 0.22.0+** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/6535

I'm not thrilled that this patch is still relying on the `.daemon()` thing, and worse, now we're setting it on a private attribute `._thread`.   

Shouldn't aiosqlite itself take steps to prevent the stack trace shown in the top example from ever being possible?

i dont have time today to dig into source code but with this test script:

```py
import asyncio
import aiosqlite

async def main():
    conn = await aiosqlite.connect(":memory:")
    cursor = await conn.cursor()
    await cursor.execute("select 1")
    print(f"result: {await cursor.fetchall()}")
    await cursor.close()

    print("done")


asyncio.run(main())
```

older aiosqlite prior to 0.22 hangs completely.  so that's the old thing, and that's bad.    Using 0.22.0 exactly, the program seems to exit cleanly every time, so I'm not sure how that happens whereas the SQLAlchemy version indeed continues to hang.   Using 0.22.1, the program alternatively exits cleanly or exits with a trace ending in `RuntimeError: Event loop is closed`.

This is the thing.  *sqlite itself is fully synchronous*.   I dont understand why the driver has to continue relying on event-loop systems here to close connections even in garbage collection.   if you're in garbage collection, it should **always** terminate the connection synchronously; the connection is by definition unreachable.
I think aiosqlite should set .daemon on all these threads as well.    it makes no sense that programs can just hang if a connection wasn't cleaned out, no other driver would ever do that

just to make this clear, there's absolutely no issue with the sqlite3 driver if the connection is "open" and the program just exits.   we've supported sqlite3 using this connection pool with the same method for 20 years and we've never had anyone ever report that a sqlite3 file was "corrupted" due to unclean exit.  the sqlite library is designed for an extremely wide variety of scenarios, OS'es and embedded systems and has very robust and mature recovery for things like power failures and such (see https://sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html).    I really think aiosqlite can set .daemon on threads and allow programs to simply terminate, im not enthused to have to do this on the SQLAlchemy side.
